Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor should assess whether the programs that would benefit from special taxes are spending money wisely. Supporters also want these special taxes to count toward the state spending limit, making tax rebates to Californians more likely.

The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires. Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing waste in public programs, the union says; instead it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying taxes once on their huge wealth.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor should assess whether the programs that would benefit from special taxes are spending money wisely. Supporters also want these special taxes to count toward the state spending limit, making tax rebates to Californians more likely.
Oppose
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires. Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing waste in public programs, the union says; instead it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying taxes once on their huge wealth.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”
Prop. 40 also exempts itself from the state spending limit, so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. ​ Yes on Proposition 41: Audits and Accountability for California Tax Dollars.
​
Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
​
Proposition 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs funded by any new tax measure, with results posted publicly. It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
If approved by voters, Prop 41 would require ongoing public audits to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals, and recommend improvements.

**OPPOSE POSITION: Proposition 41 — “Prohibits New State Taxes that Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit.
Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”**
On August 8, 2026, the California State PTA Board of Managers voted to approve an OPPOSE position on Proposition 41.
**What This Measure Proposes:** Proposition 41 requires a pre-election audit of any program that would receive funding from a voter-initiative special tax, recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, and prohibits new state taxes enacted after that date from being excluded from the existing voter-approved state spending limit.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 5:03 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”
Prop. 40 also exempts itself from the state spending limit, so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.

Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”
Prop. 40 also exempts itself from the state spending limit, so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

​ Yes on Proposition 41: Audits and Accountability for California Tax Dollars.
​
Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
​
Proposition 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs funded by any new tax measure, with results posted publicly. It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
If approved by voters, Prop 41 would require ongoing public audits to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals, and recommend improvements.
Learn More About Prop 41 (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41)
Endorsements
YES on Prop 41 is supported by a growing coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts.
Prop 41 is also supported by more than a million Californians who helped qualify the measure for the ballot.
Our Coalition (https://www.yesonprop41.org/)
"California families pay billions in state taxes every year and they deserve to see where that money goes and what it delivers. Proposition 41 brings real accountability and clear metrics to state spending. We're proud to support it."
Tracy Hernandez, Co-Founder and CEO of the New California Coalition
"This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending - ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone."
​
Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber
"Californians are paying more for everything, including some of the highest taxes in the country. Now more than ever, Californians deserve some relief from our state's high taxes. Prop 41 delivers."
​
Steve Westly, former Controller of California
California can't afford to keep funding programs with no accountability.
Current and former public auditors and a growing list of California residents and transparency advocates support Prop 41. Add your name to the list and join us in promoting greater accountability and better results.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 5:03 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”

​ Yes on Proposition 41: Audits and Accountability for California Tax Dollars.
​
Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
​
Proposition 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs funded by any new tax measure, with results posted publicly. It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
If approved by voters, Prop 41 would require ongoing public audits to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals, and recommend improvements.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. The Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide (VIG).
Voter Initiative Process. California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process. Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot. State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot. Supporters notify the Secretary of State once they have gathered 25 percent of the necessary signatures.
Special Taxes. State taxes can be raised by the Legislature or by voters. When a “special tax” is created, the revenue from that tax is dedicated to a specific purpose or program. For example, certain fuel taxes can only be used to pay for public roads and other transportation programs.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments follow the law, use money, and run their programs. These reviews are called audits. An audit may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly over time while other audits are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process. This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit. If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be included in the VIG. If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.
Ongoing Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From New or Increased Special Taxes. Proposition 41 also requires the State Auditor to periodically review programs that receive funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. These ongoing audits would happen every four years. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor will include in these audits, including recommendations to improve program efficiency. Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of this ongoing work will be paid using the new tax revenue.
State Appropriations Limit. The State Constitution limits how much tax revenues the state can spend each year. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes and special taxes. However, certain types of spending, for example for infrastructure, are excluded from this limit. Under Proposition 41, the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the limit.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Auditor Costs, Mostly Paid by New Revenues. Proposition 41 would increase State Auditor costs by creating new and ongoing audit requirements. The costs would depend on (1) the number of new or increased special taxes that are proposed and approved and (2) the complexity of the programs being audited. These costs likely would be in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time. The one-time and ongoing audit costs associated with special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature would be paid from the revenues collected by the special taxes. One-time audit costs associated with special taxes that do not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters would be paid from the state’s General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. Proposition 41 would require a summary of the State Auditor’s review to appear in the VIG when a voter initiative with a special tax appears on the ballot. These audit summaries could add several pages to the VIG, which would increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Possible Savings if State Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to make recommendations for programs to reduce costs or improve efficiency. Proposition 41 could result in savings or improved services if policymakers implement the State Auditor’s recommendations and those recommendations prove effective. Any resulting savings would depend on future decisions and are not known.
Net Effect Not Known. The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 41
CALIFORNIANS DESERVE BETTER RESULTS FOR OUR TAX DOLLARS
Prop. 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct independent public audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes in order to increase transparency and accountability and drive better outcomes.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country-on top of our high cost of living. This year alone, California’s state government will spend more than $350 billion-a 79% increase in spending since 2019. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it.
We deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop. 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Here’s how Prop. 41 works.
PUBLIC AUDITS TO PROVIDE ACCOUNTABILITY, TRANSPARENCY AND OVERSIGHT
Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct performance and financial audits of the programs funded by new tax measures, with the results posted publicly. The audits must:
• Track all program spending and assess whether it’s achieving its intended outcomes; • Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability; • Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; • Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and programs made more effective.
Prop. 41 requires audits both before taxes are voted on to provide transparency to voters, and ongoing audits of programs funded by approved taxes to ensure accountability. PROP. 41: INDEPENDENT, PUBLIC INFORMATION FOR VOTERS ON PROPOSED TAXES
Before we vote on new taxes to fund programs, voters should have access to independent information about how those programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Under Prop. 41, the Auditor’s findings must be posted publicly and in the Voter Information Guide-so voters can make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
“This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending- ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone.” -Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce
PROP. 41: A BETTER DEAL FOR TAXPAYERS
Prop. 41 doesn’t raise taxes-it protects taxpayers’ interests:
• Reduces the waste and fraud that have cost California taxpayers billions of dollars in recent years; • Requires all taxes to comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit-including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Prop. 41 ensures taxpayers get better results-not just a bigger tax bill.
“Every tax dollar we waste is a dollar that could actually help someone. Californians already pay the highest state income and sales taxes in the country-we need better transparency and accountability to make sure our tax dollars produce results. Prop. 41 delivers.” -Steve Westly, former Controller of California.
Please join good government groups, small business owners, accountants, taxpayers and public transparency advocates in voting Yes on 41.
For more information, visit: www.ResultsCA.org

## What Prop. 41 Would Do
Proposition 41 would require the state auditor, working with the Legislative Analyst’s Office, to conduct an independent review of any state-level citizen initiative that aims to create a new special tax once it reaches 25% of the required signature threshold to be placed on the ballot.
(Special taxes differ from general taxes in that they dedicate revenue to a specific purpose.)
All new state-level special taxes would be audited every four years.
Additionally, any new special taxes passed after January 1, 2026 — whether proposed through legislation or through voter initiatives — would be subject to the Gann Limit, a voter-imposed revenue spending limit explained in the Backstory section below.
The audit of proposed citizen initiatives would examine the individual programs that would receive funding through the special tax and assess whether the programs are sufficiently cost-efficient in their hiring and operating practices.

The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.
